naslov: Windhorst & MacMahon: What league insiders are seeing from Philly's 8-1 start
tekst:
Early in the NBA season, bad surprises receive more attention than the good ones.
For teams in the occasional negative spotlight, it's annoying and they often complain about it and quite fairly. But it's the nature of a high-profile, high-stakes business. And there will be plenty of that in this weekly space, but this week there's a pull toward some of the more pleasant developments with the 2026-27 season in its third week.
The advance scouts and pro personnel directors have made their first loops and filed their initial reports. Assistant coaches have seen the first rounds of film as they prepare for opponents.
We've talked to them and others and here's some of what they're saying about two of the hottest teams in the league, plus the next steps for 
What is the league making of the Philadelphia 76ers' start?
Brian Windhorst: The term superteam is often overused, but with five Most Valuable Player awards and five Finals MVP awards on this roster, it qualifies.
Historically, superteams see their offense lag behind their defense early as stars settle into their roles. This was true of the 2007-08 Boston Celtics, who averaged just 93.5 points over their first 10 games but were No. 1 on defense from day one. In 2010-11, the Miami Heat had a top-five defense right away but sluggish offensive nights contributed to a 9-8 start.
Add the 2026-27 Sixers to the list, with Philly languishing in the bottom 10 in offensive efficiency but boasting a top-three defense. That stinginess is a major reason for the 76ers' 4-0 road record, including wins against the New York Knicks on opening night and Detroit Pistons on Wednesday.
And LeBron James, Jaylen Brown, Joel Embiid and Tyrese Maxey are owning clutch time.
"They've been terrific in the clutch and I haven't seen much clunkiness or indecisiveness in them at all in the games I've watched," an Eastern Conference scout told ESPN. "They also aren't turning the ball over, which you expect to see with a bunch of new guys playing together."
The 76ers are 7-0 this season in games that have entered clutch time -- defined as the score being within five points in the final five minutes -- the driving force of their league-best 8-1 record. It's not prudent to jump to conclusions or to overanalyze it, but it's fair to say it has been a very good sign. And league personnel have a reason.
"It's Maxey," an East executive said. "He's making them go and you can see he already has all of their trust in fourth quarters. LeBron definitely trusts him and they've already really developed a nice two-man game that stresses defenses."
Another East executive said, "LeBron brings a lot of things when he comes to your team. And we've seen it before, he raises everyone's level. Maxey was already a great player, but he's also raised his level and some of that has to be having LeBron there."
Tim MacMahon: There were a lot of questions -- and doubts -- around the league about how the Sixers' four All-Stars would mesh.
As much as egos were considered a potential obstacle, it has been interesting to see Maxey, the least decorated of the quartet, emerge as the clear No. 1 option. He has been the primary reason that Philadelphia keeps pulling out close wins, ranking third in the league with 21 points in 19 clutch minutes.
"He comes and gets the first bucket or two of the fourth and ... 'Here it comes, here it comes,'" 76ers coach Nick Nurse said of the 26-year-old guard. "In an incredibly humble way, he just seems like he knows he's really good. I don't know if I've sensed that until this year."
Windhorst: Another factor league insiders have noticed is the working relationship James already has built with his new coach.
They didn't have a previous relationship, but James and Nurse had an extensive conversation before James chose the 76ers in free agency. They talked several times before the start of training camp, establishing an important base. That might seem like something that would be taken for granted. Considering James' history when joining a new team, it shouldn't.
"LeBron didn't vibe with [Heat coach Erik Spoelstra] at the start, and lots of people think he wanted him fired in the first month [of 2010-11]," one veteran NBA executive said. "He never gave David Blatt a chance (when James went back to the Cleveland Cavaliers) and it went sideways really quick when he went to L.A. with Luke [Walton].
"From the outside [Nurse and James] look like they're working together very well."
James has indeed shown a positive relationship with Nurse, who is tapping into the 41-year-old's versatility and buy-in. For example, James has been used as the lead ball handler for sections of the games and, conversely, had shifted to defensive center with the Sixers managing injuries to their big men. Before the season, James praised Nurse specifically for the job he did with the Toronto Raptors, who won the franchise's first title in 2019 behind Nurse's guidance.
"[LeBron] had a good relationship with JJ [Redick] from day one [with the Lakers] and they worked well together and that's a better way to live," a Western Conference assistant coach said. "If LeBron thinks you're smart and you put him in a position to be successful, he's going to respect you."
MacMahon: Major offseason additions typically force teams into roster shuffling that create other issues -- consider the Miami Heat's lack of depth after landing Giannis Antetokounmpo. But that hasn't been the case for Philadelphia, which gave up a starter in Paul George for an upgrade in Brown, then added James on a minimum deal. New Sixers president Mike Gansey also found value on the fringes, signing Anfernee Simons and Kentavious Caldwell-Pope in free agency this summer.
"Their bench is [strong] outside of a backup big," an East scout said. "Simons might be the best bench scorer in the league. KCP is really good in the role that they have for him. You add one backup big and they have an A-plus rotation."
